title: Wankel_Insights_Progress_Benjamin_Johnson
body:
Wagner's distinction of four axes of progress (touching on economic, epistemic, social, and political) reminds me of U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt's four essential human freedoms: freedom of speech, freedom of worship, freedom from want, and freedom from fear. the culmination of combining these freedoms and points of progress would eliminate war, hunger, and poverty; increase access to healthcare, education, and resources; and expand opportunity, ideological freedom, and acceptance of collective individuality. 

My views coincide most closely with Wagner's perspective. Similar to Benjamin, I think it likely that there is a long road littered with martyrs and fallen altruists, as well as collateral victims, who will be trodden under long before civilization reaches the pinnacle of progress; but where he claims that the mountain of debris is ever increasing in front of the angel of history, I tend to believe that there will be improvement in the aforementioned freedoms and progressive development axes. 

I also tend to agree with Adorno when he hypothesizes that a complete restructuring of humanity is essential to redefining and cementing the meaning of progress. The author's remarks that Adorno underestimates Social Democracy seem naive, and overly optimistic. 
For me, restructuring does not mean starting humanity over, but rather confronting the institutions of corporate domination and unchecked greed that currently define much of economic and political life. If progress is surrendered to profit-driven markets or to groups who cling to their ideals at the expense of others' peace and safety, it is not progress but exploitation. Adorno’s pessimism might be overstated, but he seems right that without a genuine redefinition, the concept of progress will remain nothing more than a mask for inequality and domination.

All three writers' views overlap where they emphasize that progress cannot simply be assumed but must be questioned, critiqued, and guided. Wagner stresses balance, Adorno exposes the hypocrisy often embedded in narratives of advancement, and Benjamin depicts progress as a perpetual accumulation of wreckage tackled in an endless cycle that never reaches culmination. Together, they remind me that progress requires vigilance, yet I still hold that the Four Freedoms, alongside Wagner’s four axes, provide a valuable framework and balanced measures that demonstrate progress is real and not merely an illusion.
